title: Hazard-Signature Tombstones: Commit-Time Forget Lockout for LLM Agent Memory

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to formalize the paraphrase re-injection vulnerability in LLM agent memory deletion and demonstrate that naive deletion backfires. This specific vulnerability — where semantically equivalent paraphrases of deleted records are re-injected under new IDs — is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While [4], [14], [16], and [17] discuss vulnerabilities in machine unlearning or relearning attacks, they do not focus on paraphrase-based re-injection as a specific mechanism of attack. Similarly, [5], [8], and [11] discuss paraphrase-based attacks, but these are aimed at evading detection or altering outputs, not exploiting memory deletion vulnerabilities. No prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship between naive deletion and increased vulnerability to paraphrase re-injection.

**Conclusion**: No prior paper establishes the same purpose.

---

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves defining the paraphrase re-injection attack, where an adversary re-inserts semantically equivalent paraphrases of deleted records under new IDs, and measuring the impact of ID-based deletion under this attack. [5], [8], and [11] describe paraphrase-based adversarial attacks, but these focus on evading detection or altering outputs, not on exploiting memory deletion vulnerabilities. [4], [14], [16], and [17] discuss vulnerabilities in machine unlearning or relearning attacks, but they do not describe paraphrase re-injection as a specific attack vector. None of the prior papers combine paraphrasing with ID-based re-injection to exploit memory deletion.

**Conclusion**: No prior paper describes an equivalent mechanism.

---

### Evaluation
The evaluation measures the poisoned retrieval proportion (PRP@3) under paraphrase re-injection, showing that naive ID-based deletion increases PRP@3 significantly. This evaluation design — measuring retrieval performance under a poisoning attack — is covered by [6], [9], [10], [12], [13], and [19], which evaluate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems under poisoning attacks. While the specific benchmark (PRP@3) and attack (paraphrase re-injection) differ, the evaluation design of measuring retrieval performance under attack is substantively equivalent. The evaluation is not novel.

**Conclusion**: Evaluation design is covered by prior work.

---

### Domain
The domain is the security of persistent LLM agent memory, specifically focusing on memory poisoning and deletion vulnerabilities. This falls under the broader area of LLM security and adversarial attacks, which is addressed by [4], [6], [9], [10], [12], [13], [14], [16], [17], and [19]. While the specific focus on paraphrase re-injection in memory deletion is new, the general domain of LLM security and adversarial attacks is well-covered.

**Conclusion**: The domain is covered by prior work.

---

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to prevent paraphrased re-injection of deleted harmful content at commit time. None of the prior papers explicitly address this objective. While papers like [2], [4], [14], and [19] discuss paraphrase detection or robustness to paraphrasing, their focus is on identifying or mitigating paraphrase attacks in text classification or detection tasks, not on preventing re-injection of harmful content during commit operations. Similarly, papers like [1] and [3] discuss tombstone-based deletion mechanisms in LSM-trees but do not address paraphrased re-injection of harmful content.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves Hazard-Signature Tombstones (HST), which extract discrete hazard signatures (structured labels over a fixed taxonomy) from deleted records and block incoming writes via fuzzy set-containment matching. Papers [1] and [3] discuss tombstone-based deletion mechanisms in LSM-trees, but these are limited to marking staleness for range deletes or compaction purposes, not for blocking paraphrased re-injection. Papers [5], [20], [21], [26], and [27] discuss fuzzy set similarity joins, Bloom filters, or approximate matching techniques, but none combine these primitives with structured hazard signatures or apply them to commit-time lockout policies. Thus, the mechanism appears novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates that fuzzy set-containment matching raises hazard-signature stability across paraphrases to 92% versus 30% for exact matching. Papers [5], [20], [21], [26], and [27] discuss evaluation designs for fuzzy set similarity joins or Bloom filters, which involve approximate matching and efficiency metrics. These designs are substantively equivalent to the evaluation design here, as they validate approximate matching techniques using stability or accuracy metrics. Therefore, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is commit-time forget/lockout policy for agent memory stores. Papers [1] and [3] discuss tombstone-based deletion mechanisms in LSM-trees, which operate in the domain of key-value storage systems. While the specific application to agent memory stores is new, the general domain of storage systems and deletion policies is covered by these prior works.
